solar_storm.title: Solar Storm Detected
solar_storm.what: A huge flare on the Sun has launched a cloud of fast protons toward the Moon. For the next 2 days, radiation at the base will be dozens of times higher than normal.
solar_storm.why: The Moon has no magnetic field and almost no atmosphere. On Earth, both shield us from solar particles — on the Moon, only walls, soil and water do.
solar_storm.principle: Shielding works by putting mass between people and radiation. Dense, hydrogen-rich material (water, regolith, polyethylene) stops solar protons best.

urgency.note: No order came in time: the crew carried on with normal operations while the particles arrived.

onTrigger.label: Solar storm: +40 mSv/day inside the habitat
Strong solar storm: about +60 mSv/day inside the habitat (scenario estimate)
Severe solar storm: about +110 mSv/day inside the habitat (scenario estimate)

options.label: Move crew into the radiation shelter
options.benefit: Blocks about 70% of the storm's radiation.
options.cost: Shelter life support uses +10 kWh/day. Nobody tends the greenhouse (half production). Electronics outside stay exposed.

effects.label: Crew in shelter: 70% of storm dose blocked

effects.benefit: Blocks about 90% of the storm's radiation.
effects.cost: Shelter life support uses +10 kWh/day. Nobody tends the greenhouse (half production). Electronics outside stay exposed.

effects.label: Crew in shelter: 90% of storm dose blocked

effects.note: A proton strike scrambled a circuit board (a 'single-event upset'): one system has failed.
effects.otherwiseNote: The base's electronics rode out the storm without damage.

effects.lesson: A dedicated shelter turns a dangerous storm into a much smaller dose — but only if you launched it, and it has a power cost.

effects.label: Build a water wall around the sleeping area
effects.benefit: Uses stored water as shielding: blocks about half of the storm dose. No water is lost.
effects.cost: Needs at least 100 kg of stored water. Crew busy moving tanks: greenhouse at half output.

effects.label: Water wall: 50% of storm dose blocked

effects.note: A proton strike scrambled a circuit board (a 'single-event upset'): one system has failed.
effects.otherwiseNote: The base's electronics rode out the storm without damage.

effects.lesson: Water is one of the best radiation shields because it is full of hydrogen. Real spacecraft designs put water tanks around crew quarters.

effects.label: Put the base in safe mode
effects.benefit: Powers down the greenhouse, oxygen generator and recycler so the storm can't damage them. Saves a lot of energy.
effects.cost: No extra protection for the crew. No food, oxygen or water recycling for 2 days.
effects.lesson: Spacecraft enter 'safe mode' to protect their electronics from radiation. It protects the machines — not the people.

effects.label: Continue normal operations
effects.benefit: Every system keeps producing at full rate.
effects.cost: The crew receives the full storm dose, and electronics can be hit.

effects.note: A proton strike scrambled a circuit board (a 'single-event upset'): one system has failed.
effects.otherwiseNote: The base's electronics rode out the storm without damage.

effects.lesson: Radiation dose adds up over a mission. A single strong storm can use up a large share of the dose a mission is planned for.

power_failure.title: Power Failure: Dust on the Solar Arrays
power_failure.what: A nearby rover landing kicked up lunar dust, which settled on the solar panels. Their output has dropped by almost half.
power_failure.why: Lunar dust (regolith) is sharp, clingy and electrically charged. With no wind or rain, nothing cleans it off.
power_failure.principle: A power system is only as good as its worst day. Engineers design for degraded performance, not just ideal conditions.

options.label: Send two astronauts outside to clean the panels
options.benefit: Panels back to 90% tomorrow and normal after that.
options.cost: A spacewalk adds radiation dose (+0.5 mSv) and takes the crew away from the greenhouse for a day.
options.lesson: Spacewalks (EVAs) solve problems fast, but every hour outside costs crew time and radiation exposure.

options.label: Let the cleaning robot do it slowly
options.benefit: No crew time and no extra radiation.
options.cost: Solar power stays at 75% for 3 days.
options.lesson: Automation saves crew time, which is the most precious resource on a mission — but it is usually slower.

options.label: Ignore it for now
options.benefit: No effort at all today.
options.cost: Solar power at 55% for 6 days while the dust slowly falls off.
options.lesson: Small problems left alone can line up with bigger ones — like dusty panels right before a shadow period.

water_leak.title: Water Leak
water_leak.what: A fitting on the main water tank cracked in the cold. 8 kg of water has already leaked, and it's still dripping.
water_leak.why: Temperatures on the Moon swing by hundreds of degrees. Metal expands and shrinks, and seals and fittings wear out.
water_leak.principle: Redundancy and spare parts turn a crisis into a routine repair.

urgency.note: No decision in time: 3 kg more water dripped away while the crew kept watching the leak.

options.label: Replace the fitting with a spare part
options.benefit: Leak fixed right away.
options.cost: Uses one spare parts kit (5 kg more water lost during the swap).
options.lesson: Spare parts are mass you hope never to use — until the day they save the mission.

options.label: Patch it with tape and sealant
options.benefit: Free, and usually slows the leak a lot.
options.cost: Still loses 4% of stored water per day for 2 days. Might fail.

effects.note: The patch didn't hold — the leak continues for 3 more days.

options.lesson: Improvised repairs are a real part of spaceflight — Apollo 13's crew famously built a CO₂ filter adapter from spare materials.

options.label: Close the valves and isolate the tank
options.benefit: Leak stops immediately and for sure.
options.cost: 20% of your stored water is trapped in the isolated tank.
options.lesson: Isolating a failed part protects the rest of the system — a key idea in spacecraft design.

options.label: Just monitor it
options.benefit: No effort or parts spent.
options.cost: Loses 8% of stored water per day for 4 days.
options.lesson: A slow leak compounds: 8% per day for 4 days loses about 28% of your water.

equipment_failure.title: Equipment Failure
equipment_failure.what: A pump failed inside one of your life-support machines. It has shut down.
equipment_failure.why: Pumps, fans and valves run non-stop. On the ISS, life-support parts are regularly replaced because they wear out.
equipment_failure.principle: Reliability engineering: every part will fail eventually. Plan for repairs and keep critical systems redundant.

options.label: Install a new pump from the spare parts kit
options.benefit: System back online right away.
options.cost: Uses one spare parts kit.
options.lesson: Carrying spares for the most failure-prone parts is standard practice for ISS life support.

options.label: Try to repair the old pump
options.benefit: Free if it works.
options.cost: Only a 50% chance to work.

effects.note: The repair worked — the system is back online!
effects.otherwiseNote: The repair failed. The system stays offline — you can try again from the Systems panel.

options.lesson: Being able to repair things on site makes a crew far less dependent on Earth.

options.label: Leave it off for now
options.benefit: Saves its power for other systems.
options.cost: No production until you repair it from the Systems panel.
options.lesson: Turning a broken system off saves power, but your stored supplies now have to cover the gap.

crop_failure.title: Crop Failure
crop_failure.what: A root disease is spreading through the greenhouse. The plants are wilting.
crop_failure.why: In a closed greenhouse, microbes spread fast through shared water. There are no natural predators to keep them in check.
crop_failure.principle: Biological systems are productive but less predictable than machines. Missions keep stored food as a backup.

options.label: Clear everything and replant
options.benefit: Healthy plants again, full output once they grow.
options.cost: No harvest for the next 7 days while new plants grow. Uses 10 kg of water to sterilize.
options.lesson: Restarting a biological system takes time — that's why growth time matters when planning food.

options.label: Treat the plants and hope
options.benefit: Keeps some production going.
options.cost: Only 40% output for 4 days, and the treatment system uses +5 kWh/day.
options.lesson: Partial output is often better than none — but it comes with its own costs.

options.label: Shut the greenhouse down
options.benefit: Frees 40 kWh/day of power and 2 kg/day of water.
options.cost: No more fresh food or plant oxygen (you can switch it back on, but it restarts from zero).
options.lesson: Sometimes the best engineering decision is to cut your losses and redirect resources.

oxygen_leak.title: Emergency: Oxygen Leak
oxygen_leak.what: Cabin pressure is dropping. Inside the life-support bay, a seal where an oxygen line passes through the hull has cracked, and air is hissing out: 4 kg of oxygen are already gone.
oxygen_leak.why: The habitat keeps air at the same pressure as on Earth, with vacuum on the other side of the wall. Every seal is pushed outward all the time, and the cold makes rubber stiff and brittle.
oxygen_leak.principle: Hatches split a spacecraft into compartments. Closing one cuts a leak off from the crew: ISS crews have closed hatches module by module to hunt down slow leaks.

urgency.note: Nobody gave an order in time. 2 kg more oxygen escaped before the pressure sensors closed the bay hatch on their own.

options.label: Repair the leak right now
options.benefit: If it works, the leak is gone and every compartment stays in use.
options.cost: Opening the panel lets 1 kg more escape. With a spare kit it almost always works (90%); without one it is a gamble (45%).

then.note: The new seal from the spare kit is holding. Cabin pressure is back to normal.
then.otherwiseNote: The new seal did not seat properly: a slow leak continues for 2 days.

else.note: No spare seal, but the improvised patch of sealant and tape is holding.
else.otherwiseNote: No spare seal, and the improvised patch blew out under pressure. The leak is worse for 3 days.

options.lesson: In 2018 an ISS crew found a 2 mm hole in their Soyuz and sealed it with epoxy and gauze. Fast repairs work best with the right parts at hand.

options.label: Seal off the life-support bay
options.benefit: Closing the hatch cuts the leak off from the crew. With power, the motorised hatch seals for sure.
options.cost: The air left in the bay is lost to the crew (15% of stored oxygen). The oxygen generator feeds the cabin through the bay: only half its output arrives for 3 days. With empty batteries the hatch is closed by hand (60%).

effects.label: Life-support bay sealed: oxygen generator at 50%

otherwise.label: Hatch closed by hand, not airtight: -4% oxygen/day

else.note: With the batteries empty, the crew cranked the hatch shut by hand. It is airtight.
else.otherwiseNote: With the batteries empty, the crew cranked the hatch shut by hand, but it is not fully airtight: a slow leak continues for 2 days.

options.lesson: Compartments are a spacecraft's safety net: a leak behind a closed hatch can no longer reach the crew.

options.label: Move the crew to the shelter module
options.benefit: The crew breathes safely in the shelter while the empty habitat is resealed and refilled. The leak is fixed for sure.
options.cost: Refilling the habitat uses 6 kg of oxygen. Shelter life support needs +10 kWh/day and the greenhouse is left alone (50%) for a day.
options.lesson: The first rule of an emergency is to keep the crew safe. Machines can be fixed later; people cannot be replaced.

options.label: Run the leak diagnostics first
options.benefit: Ultrasonic sensors find the exact crack, so your next move is far more likely to work.
options.cost: Air keeps escaping while the scan runs: 2 kg more oxygen lost. Then you still have to choose a fix.
options.lesson: Finding a leak is often harder than fixing it. In 2020 the ISS crew used ultrasonic detectors, and even floating tea leaves, to find a tiny leak.

oxygen_leak_located.title: Leak Located
oxygen_leak_located.what: Diagnostics found it: a 3 cm crack in the hull seal of an oxygen line, inside the life-support bay. Air is still escaping.
oxygen_leak_located.why: Escaping air makes ultrasound: far too high for human ears, but easy for a sensor to hear and point at.
oxygen_leak_located.principle: Good information turns a gamble into an engineering decision.

urgency.note: Nobody gave an order in time. 2 kg more oxygen escaped before the pressure sensors closed the bay hatch on their own.

options.label: Replace the cracked seal
options.benefit: You know exactly where to work. With a spare kit the fix is certain; without one, a targeted patch works 75% of the time.
options.cost: Uses one spare kit if you have one.

otherwise.label: Patch leaking at one edge: -6% oxygen/day

else.note: No spare seal, but the patch over the crack is holding.
else.otherwiseNote: No spare seal, and the patch leaks at one edge: a slow leak continues for 2 days.

options.lesson: Diagnose, then repair: knowing the exact failure lets a crew use the smallest, surest fix.

options.label: Seal off the life-support bay
options.benefit: Closing the hatch cuts the leak off from the crew. With power, the motorised hatch seals for sure.
options.cost: The air left in the bay is lost to the crew (15% of stored oxygen). The oxygen generator feeds the cabin through the bay: only half its output arrives for 3 days. With empty batteries the hatch is closed by hand (60%).

effects.label: Life-support bay sealed: oxygen generator at 50%

otherwise.label: Hatch closed by hand, not airtight: -4% oxygen/day

else.note: With the batteries empty, the crew cranked the hatch shut by hand. It is airtight.
else.otherwiseNote: With the batteries empty, the crew cranked the hatch shut by hand, but it is not fully airtight: a slow leak continues for 2 days.

options.lesson: Compartments are a spacecraft's safety net: a leak behind a closed hatch can no longer reach the crew.
